title: T1078.002 — Valid Accounts - Domain Accounts
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Valid Accounts - Domain Accounts with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Animated diagram of a domain account attack: an attacker phishes domain user a.chen through a fake portal, logs in to the VPN, queries the domain controller, opens file shares, abuses a service account on member servers, triggers SOC correlation, and is stopped by disabling accounts and isolating servers.

steps.title: The phish
steps.caption: Domain user a.chen receives a realistic email about an expiring password. She clicks through to a fake SSO portal that mirrors the company login page. She types her domain username and password, and the site quietly forwards them to the attacker's server. At this point no security tool fires an alert, because nothing touched the company yet
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: VPN login
steps.caption: From a rented residential proxy, the attacker opens the company VPN portal and signs in as a.chen. The VPN accepts the password because it is correct - no exploit needed. The session lands inside the network with the same rights a.chen has. The VPN log now shows a sign-in from a new network provider and a country she never works from
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: Enumeration
steps.caption: Using the VPN session, the attacker runs directory queries against the domain controller. Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) calls list groups, admin accounts, service accounts, and file share names. The directory answers politely - it cannot tell a curious employee from an attacker. The DC logs an unusual volume of directory access events from this one session
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: Share access
steps.caption: The valid account now opens department file shares exactly like an employee would. The attacker lists folders in bulk and opens documents that look interesting: password sheets, finance files, onboarding notes. The share audit trail shows mass reads from one user at an unusual hour
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: Service account hit
steps.caption: The attacker requests Kerberos service tickets for accounts with Service Principal Names (SPNs) and finds svc_report . Its password is weak and reused, so the attacker logs into a member server with it. Defenders see two signals at once: a spike of TGS requests (4769), and an interactive logon (4624) for an account that should only ever run services
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: Privilege attempt
steps.caption: The same service password works on two more servers, because teams copied the same password years ago. The attacker now touches several machines in minutes, all from one source address. Successful logon storms like this are the clearest lateral movement shape in Windows logs
steps.defender: IdP and SaaS audit logs record token issuance, consent, sign-in location and API access.

steps.title: SOC alert
steps.caption: No single alert was loud, but correlation changes that: VPN anomaly plus TGS spike plus service-account interactive logon equals one incident. The analyst pulls the timeline and sees the full path from phish to servers. The case moves from "odd logon" to confirmed intrusion in one view

steps.title: Response
steps.caption: The team disables a.chen and svc_report , resets their passwords, and isolates the affected member servers. They plan a two-part krbtgt password rotation because domain credential exposure is possible. Recovery starts only after the scope is clear and evidence is saved
